title: Still, sparkling and decanting at the exam
lead: The Court's service mechanics at Certified standard: setup, the order, still and sparkling wine, decanting, after-dinner drinks and serving temperatures.

intro.title: FOUR WAYS TO SERVE
intro.text: From Level 1: present, open, taste, pour. Here is each service the Court defines, the way the examiners want to see it.

sections.name: Mise en place and traywork

lines.label: Your kit
lines.text: Two openers, two pens, a pad of paper and two odorless lighters or matches.

lines.label: The rule
lines.text: Only stemware touches the tablecloth. Bottles, decanters and corks sit on underliners.

know: Polish glasses with clean linen over steam; they must be spotless and odor-free.
Serviettes are cotton (they must not repel water) and folded before service.
Bring glasses and service items to the table on a tray lined with a napkin.
Fill an ice bucket with water and ice so the bottle slides in and out without overflowing.
Stemware, tools and carrying a tray of stemware are all scored.

visuals.title: The sommelier's kit
visuals.note: At the exam, bring the opener, pen and notepad; the rest is provided.

sections.name: The order and the glasses

lines.label: The order
lines.text: Take it from the host's right and repeat it back. The host is whoever orders the wine.

lines.label: The glasses
lines.text: Set from the guest's right, keyed off the knife, the same way for every guest, starting with the host or the person to the host's left.

know: Several glasses can go in a line, diagonal, diamond or cluster: just be consistent.
A new wine's glass goes to the right of earlier glasses, so you never pour over stemware.
A second bottle of the same wine: give the host a fresh glass for the taste, then clear it.
Present the bottle on a serviette in your hand or on your forearm, and repeat the name and vintage.
Serviettes never go in a pocket or on your shoulder.

items.text: From the host's right; repeat it

items.name: Set glasses
items.text: From the right, keyed off the knife, clockwise

items.name: Underliners
items.text: Right of or in front of the host

items.name: Present
items.text: Bottle on a serviette; name and vintage

sections.name: Opening still wine

lines.label: White
lines.text: Four methods: in hand, in the bucket, on an underliner at the table or side station, or on a gueridon. Then into the bucket or onto an underliner at the host's right.

lines.label: Young red
lines.text: Three methods: in hand, on an underliner at the table or side station, or on a gueridon. Then onto an underliner at the host's right.

know: Cut the foil at the second or lower lip, pocket it, and wipe the cork top.
Pull the cork quietly, with as little bottle movement as possible.
Wipe the bottle top, then present the cork on an underliner to the host's right.
A screwcap goes in your pocket, unpresented. Wipe the lip and carry on.
Treat a synthetic cork exactly like a natural one.

sections.name: Pouring to exam standard

lines.label: The taste
lines.text: Right hand, label to the host, a 1 to 1.5 oz taste. Step back and wait for approval.

lines.label: The table
lines.text: Then pour clockwise, moving to the host's left. A guest of honor is served first.

know: Still wine: up to half full, depending on the glass.
Wipe the bottle after every pour so it doesn't drip.
Leave the bottle on an underliner or in a bucket within the host's reach.
Ask before you remove the cork.
Scored: correct glass, clockwise, no drips, the host taste, pace and pour height.

sections.name: Sparkling wine service

lines.label: Three methods
lines.text: Always present in the air. Then open in the air, in the bucket on its stand, or in the air at a gueridon or side station.

lines.label: Control
lines.text: A serviette over the cage and cork, your hand never off the top, the bottle always pointed away from guests.

know: Cut the foil at the bottom of the cage with the corkscrew blade. The tab is allowed, not preferred.
Loosen the cage but don't take it off until the cork is out.
Twist the bottle, not the cork, at 45 degrees. Never brace it against your body.
Ease the cork out quietly until the rush of CO2 fades.
Pour up to 3/4 full, evenly, one glass at a time, in two pours at most.

items.name: Prepare
items.text: Tulips or flutes, bucket and stand, two serviettes

items.name: Foil
items.text: Cut at the bottom of the cage with the blade

items.name: Cage
items.text: Loosen, keep it on, thumb on top

items.name: Cork
items.text: Twist the bottle at 45°, release quietly

items.name: Pour
items.text: Up to 3/4, max two pours per glass

sections.name: Decanting an old red

lines.label: The setup
lines.text: Everything goes on a gueridon before it comes to the table: decanter, lighter, three serviettes, three underliners, candle or flashlight, cork tools and a decanting basket.

lines.label: Why decant
lines.text: Young wines are decanted for air. Old wines are decanted to leave the sediment behind.

know: Carry the bottle in a lined basket without disturbing the sediment.
Not stored label up? Leave it as is, explain, and show the label after decanting.
Light the candle away from the table when you can.
Pour in one smooth movement; stop when sediment reaches the shoulder. Never look away.
Taste the host from the decanter, then ask about the cork and the empty bottle.

items.name: YOUNG BORDEAUX
items.text: For air; aged Bordeaux for sediment

items.name: VINTAGE PORT
items.text: Old vintage and single quinta, for sediment

sections.name: After-dinner drinks

lines.label: The setup
lines.text: Cordials, Port and brandy are sold and served from a gueridon or tray, with everything on it before you reach the table.

lines.label: Two methods
lines.text: Measure with a jigger at the gueridon and present the glass on a lined tray from the right. Or bring glass, bottle and serviette on a tray and pour at the table.

know: Bring jiggers, a lined tray, the bottles, the right glasses and three serviettes.
Offer help choosing; talk styles, countries and pairings with desserts and cheeses.
Sweet and fortified wines by the glass are usually a 2 oz pour.
Old vintage and single quinta Ports need decanting for sediment.
Spirits and fortified wines are stored standing up.

items.label: METHOD 1
items.title: Pour at the gueridon
items.text:
Measure with a jigger
Pour into the right glass
Present on a lined tray, from the right

items.label: METHOD 2
items.title: Pour at the table
items.text:
Glass, bottle and serviette on a lined tray
Glass to the guest's right
Pour the proper amount

sections.name: Temperatures by style

lines.label: The exam standard
lines.text: The Court sets serving ranges 'for exam standards'. In real service the style and the guest decide.

lines.label: Beyond wine
lines.text: The ranges cover fortified wines and beer too.

know: Sparkling, light whites, sweet whites and mineral water: 42-50°F.
Full-bodied reds are warmest: 58-65°F.
Dry Sherry and dry Madeira: 48-55°F. Tawny Port, sweet Sherry, sweet Madeira, vintage Port: 55-62°F.
Lager and pilsner: 40-45°F. Porter, stout and English ale: 50-55°F.
Long-term storage: a constant 50-60°F.

mixups.why: Still: cut at the second or lower lip. Sparkling: cut at the bottom of the cage with the corkscrew blade.
Still: up to half full, depending on the glass. Sparkling: up to 3/4, in no more than two pours.
Young: for air. Old: to leave the sediment behind.
White has four (including opening in the ice bucket). Young red has three and ends on an underliner.

facts.fact: Required sommelier tools: 2 wine bottle openers, 2 pens, 1 pad of paper, 2 odorless lighters or matches.

Mise en place: wine lists clean, correct, current, easy to read; glassware clean, spotless, odor-free, polished with clean linen using steam; serviettes of cotton or similar that don't repel water, folded before service; underliners cleaned and polished; trays, ice buckets, stands and decanters clean and ready; opening tools organized.
Glass stemware is the only thing to touch the tablecloth; bottles, decanters and corks go on an underliner. Glassware and service items are brought to the table on a tray lined with a napkin.

The Court's example feedback report scores Mise en Place (Other Equipment & Tools, Stemware), Opening (Confident, Quiet, Presentation, Safe, Wipes Bottle Lip, Opening Sparkling Wine), Order Taking (Repeat Order, Tracks Order Correctly), Pouring (Correct Glassware, Clockwise Service, No Drips, Offers Host Approval Taste, Pace, Pour Height) and Traywork (Pace, Tray Carry with Stemware).

Beverage service is always on the guest's right. The wine list is presented and assistance offered. The order is taken from the host's right and repeated to confirm. The host is the person who orders the wine.

Glassware is placed from the guest's right, consistently, starting with the host or the person to the host's left and continuing clockwise regardless of gender. Space permitting, underliners for bottle, cork and decanters go to the right of and/or in front of the host.

The sommelier presents the bottle and repeats the name and vintage. The bottle is presented underlined by a serviette held in hand or on the forearm. Serviettes are in hand or on the forearm during all service, never in pockets or on the shoulder.

Glassware placement: right size and shape for each wine; placed to the guest's right and keyed off the knife; multiple glasses in a line, diagonal, diamond or cluster; consistent among all guests. A second bottle of the same wine gets a fresh tasting glass for the host, placed right of the first and cleared afterward; be ready to replace all glasses if asked. New wines' glasses go to the right of earlier ones so you never pour over stemware.

Still wine: foil cut at the second or lower lip so wine can't drip behind it; foil into the pocket; cork top wiped; cork removed with minimal movement and as quietly as possible; bottle top wiped; cork presented to the host's right on an underliner.

The bottle is held in the right hand, label to the host, for a 1 to 1.5 ounce taste; the sommelier steps back and waits. After approval, serve moving to the host's left (clockwise); a guest of honor is served first, then clockwise regardless of gender. Wipe the bottle after each pour. Place the bottle on an underliner or in an ice bucket within the host's reach, without hindering movement. Ask to remove the cork.

White wine service has four methods: open in hand; open in a bucket to the host's right; open on an underliner on the table or a side station; open on a gueridon near the table, preferably to the host's right. Afterward the bottle goes in an ice bucket or on an underliner to the host's right. Glasses are filled up to 1/2 full depending on stemware size.

Young red wine service has three methods: open in hand; open on an underliner on the table or at a side station; open on a gueridon near the table. The bottle then goes on an underliner to the host's right. Glasses are filled up to 1/2 full depending on stemware size.
Screwcaps: present as standard, remove as quietly as possible, put the cap in your pocket (it is not presented), wipe the lip, pour the host's taste. Synthetic corks are treated like natural corks.

Sparkling methods: present in the air and open in the air; present in the air and open in a bucket and stand; present in the air and open in the air at a gueridon or side station. Prepare glasses, ice bucket, stand and two serviettes; the bottle properly chilled; bucket filled with water and ice so the bottle moves in and out without overflowing; bucket to the host's right without blocking service.

Sparkling: tulips or flutes placed from a lined tray; cork and bottle underliners to the host's right; ice bucket with stand to the host's right with a clean serviette on top or in its handle; present and re-confirm the order.

Sparkling: cut the foil cleanly at the bottom of the cage with the corkscrew blade (the tab is allowed but not preferred); foil into the pocket; clean serviette held firmly over cage and cork; always point the bottle away from guests; untwist and loosen the cage but do not remove it; keep hand or thumb over cage and cork; twist the bottle, not the cork, at 45 degrees, in the air or against the inside of the bucket, never against the body; release the cork as quietly as possible until the rush of CO2 dissipates.

Sparkling: cage into the pocket, cork on the underliner to the host's right, wipe the lip thoroughly. Hold the bottle in the right hand or by the bottom (not the punt); two fingers under the neck is acceptable. Label to the host, 1 to 1.5 ounce taste, serviette against drips. After approval, pour in standard order. Fill evenly up to 3/4 full, one glass at a time, with a maximum of two pours per glass. Bottle goes in the ice bucket or on an underliner per the host's preference; ask to remove the cork and unused underliner.

Curriculum Guide (Champagne, Certified column): never point the cork at someone while opening, and never take your hand off the top (cage and cork) while removing the cork; follow the CMS-A sparkling opening standards.

Old red wine service: a gueridon or room service cart is used for decanting, with all materials on it before going tableside. Items: clean decanter, matches or odorless lighter, three serviettes, three underliners (cork, bottle, decanter), candle or small flashlight, cork removal tools, decanting basket.

Decanting: line the basket with a clean serviette and take it to the cellar; place the bottle in it without disturbing sediment; if not stored label up, leave it as is, present it with an explanation, decant, then show the label. Light the candle away from the table when possible. Roll the gueridon to the table, preferably to the host's right. Prop the basket with an underliner or serviette if its angle is too low.

Decanting: remove the foil at the second lip (whole foil acceptable but not preferred; tell the guest if so); remove the cork with whatever tool is needed; wipe the lip a second time; pour slowly into the decanter in one smooth movement, bottle a safe distance above the flame, using the light to watch the shoulder; never look away; stop once fine or gross sediment reaches the shoulder; don't touch the bottle to the decanter.

After decanting: wipe drips; bottle and cork on underliners with the label to the host; pour the host a 1 to 1.5 ounce taste from the decanter and ask if the wine can be served; serve in standard manner; wipe the decanter after each pour; decanter on an underliner within the host's reach; ask about removing the cork and the bottle; remove unused underliners.
Curriculum Guide (Bordeaux, Certified column): decant young Bordeaux for aeration and aged Bordeaux for sediment; service temperatures.
Curriculum Guide (California North Coast): young Cabernet Sauvignon often benefits from decanting; old Cabernet Sauvignon needs decanting for sediment.
Decant young Brunello di Montalcino (Curriculum Guide, Tuscany).
Young Taurasi and Sagrantino di Montefalco should be decanted (Curriculum Guide, Central & Southern Italy).
Old Vintage and Single Quinta Ports require decanting for sediment; by-the-glass fortified pours are typically 2 oz (Curriculum Guide, Fortified Wines).

Cordial, Port and Brandy service: a gueridon or tray is used for after-dinner drinks, with everything on it before going tableside. Items: measuring jiggers, lined service tray, beverage selections, appropriate glassware, three serviettes. Offer help choosing and answer questions on styles, countries of origin, and pairings with desserts and cheeses. Method 1: measure with a jigger on the gueridon, pour, and present on a lined tray from the right. Method 2: bring glass, bottle and a clean serviette on a lined tray; place the glass to the guest's right and pour the proper amount.
Sweet wines by the glass: usually a 2 oz serving; open bottles can typically last about a week kept cold in the refrigerator (Curriculum Guide, Sweet Wines).
Storage: constant temperature, 50-60°F / 10-15°C ideal for long-term storage; cork-finished table wines on their side; spirits and fortified wines standing up.

Suggested serving temperatures 'for exam standards': mineral water, sweet white, Champagne and sparkling, light-bodied white 42-50°F (5.5-10°C); dry Sherry and dry Madeira 48-55°F (9-13°C); dry rosé 45-55°F (7-13°C); full-bodied white and light-bodied red 50-59°F (10-15°C); medium-bodied red 55-62°F (13-17°C); full-bodied red 58-65°F (14.5-18°C); tawny Port, sweet Sherry, sweet Madeira and vintage Port 55-62°F (13-17°C). They are guidelines; style and preference decide in the end.

Beer serving temperatures: lager and pilsner 40-45°F (4.5-7°C); specialty ale (Belgian pale, wheat, APA, IPA, cream, abbey) 45-50°F (7-10°C); English-style ale, cask-conditioned ale, porter and stout, Belgian dubbel 50-55°F (10-13°C); lambic 45-50°F (7-10°C).
Curriculum Guide (Germany, Certified column): know styles and sweetness levels, where each belongs on a wine list, and appropriate serving temperatures.
Possible service exam scenarios include opening sparkling wine and serving guests, opening and pouring wines by the glass, and serving a wine flight.
In the mock restaurant role play, watch reaching over a guest's space.
The Certified expected skill set includes proficiency in tableside service: still and sparkling wine bottle and glass pour service.

unverified: Pour height is a scored line in the Court's example feedback report, but the Service Standards give no height; none is stated here.
The Standards say to serve 'moving to the left (clockwise) of the host' but don't say whether the host's own glass is filled first or last; not stated here.
The Curriculum Guide gives the 2 oz fortified pour as both 59.1 ml (sweet wines) and 51.9 ml (fortified wines); only '2 oz' is used.
Wine Folly's temperature video may give ranges that differ from the Court's; the chapter's numbers are the Court's.

stops.text: Bucket and stand **to the host’s right**, a clean serviette on top. Cork and bottle **underliners** to the host’s right. Present the bottle **in the air** and re-confirm the order.

stops.name: Foil and cage
stops.text: Cut the foil at the **bottom of the cage** with the corkscrew blade. A serviette goes over the cage and cork. **Loosen the cage but leave it on**; your hand never leaves the top.

stops.name: The cork
stops.text: Hold the bottle at **45 degrees**, pointed away from guests, and **twist the bottle, not the cork**. Do it in the air or against the inside of the bucket, never against your body. Release it **quietly**.

stops.name: The pour
stops.text: Hold the bottle in your right hand or by the bottom (not the punt). Host’s taste first. Then fill evenly **up to 3/4**, one glass at a time, **two pours at most**.

read.mixup: **Still** foil is cut at the **second lip**. **Sparkling** foil is cut at the **bottom of the cage**.
read.sayIt: To start the evening, the Champagne. Shall I pour?

read.bigIdea: Slow, steady, eyes on the shoulder.
read.where: The Court’s **old red wine service** happens at a **gueridon** (a side cart) or room service cart. Everything goes on it **before** you go to the table.

stops.name: From the cellar
stops.text: Line the **decanting basket** with a serviette and lay the bottle in **without disturbing the sediment**. If it wasn’t stored label up, leave it; explain, and show the label after decanting.

stops.name: At the table
stops.text: Light the **candle away from the table**. Roll the gueridon to the **host’s right** and present the bottle in its basket. Cut the foil at the **second lip**, pull the cork, wipe the lip twice.

stops.name: The pour
stops.text: One **smooth movement**, bottle a safe distance above the flame. Watch the **shoulder** in the light and **stop when sediment reaches it**. Never look away; don’t touch bottle to decanter.

stops.name: Serve
stops.text: Bottle and cork on underliners, label to the host. A **1 to 1.5 oz taste from the decanter**, then serve. Ask whether to remove the **cork** and the **bottle**.

read.mixup: Decant a **young** wine for **air**. Decant an **old** wine for **sediment**.
read.sayIt: This wine has some sediment, so I’ll decant it for you.

read.bigIdea: Measured pours, from a gueridon or tray.
read.where: The Court’s **cordial, Port and brandy service** runs from a **gueridon or tray**. Bring **jiggers, a lined tray, the bottles, the right glassware and three serviettes**.

stops.name: Sell it
stops.text: Offer help choosing. Talk **styles, countries of origin** and pairings with **desserts and cheeses**.

stops.name: Method 1
stops.text: At the gueridon, **measure with a jigger**, pour, and present the glass on a lined tray **from the right**.

stops.name: Method 2
stops.text: Bring glass, bottle and a clean serviette on a lined tray. Set the glass **to the guest’s right** and pour the proper amount.

stops.name: Pour size
stops.text: Sweet and fortified wines by the glass are usually **2 oz**. Old vintage and single quinta **Ports need decanting** for sediment.

read.sayIt: Would anyone like a glass of Port or a digestif with dessert?

keyPoints.line: for sparkling, light whites and sweet whites.
for full-bodied reds, the warmest wines.
for tawny and vintage Port, sweet Sherry, Madeira.
for lager and pilsner, the coldest beer.

read.bigIdea: Cold for light and fizzy, cool for big reds.
read.where: From Level 1: you saw the ranges. At Certified they are the **exam standard**, and the theory curriculum asks for serving temperatures in places like **Bordeaux** and **Germany**.

stops.name: Coldest
stops.text: **Sparkling, light whites, sweet whites** and mineral water: **42-50°F** (5.5-10°C). Dry rosé: **45-55°F**.

stops.name: Cool
stops.text: **Dry Sherry and dry Madeira**: **48-55°F**. **Full whites and light reds**: **50-59°F**.

stops.name: Warmer
stops.text: **Medium reds**, **tawny and vintage Port**, **sweet Sherry and sweet Madeira**: **55-62°F**. **Full-bodied reds**: **58-65°F**.

stops.name: Beer
stops.text: **Lager and pilsner 40-45°F**. Specialty ales and lambic 45-50°F. **English ale, porter and stout 50-55°F**.

read.sayIt: I’ll keep the white on ice and serve the red slightly cool.
